As of 243 PM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Through tonight, the system of interest which 
has helped produce breezy south winds and mild weather today is 
a pre-frontal trough, tied to a deepening low pressure system 
over James Bay, Canada. The trough is very well defined, with a 
ribbon of glaciated cloud tops and associated rain showers 
tracking eastward over the easternmost Great Lake this 
afternoon. These showers have produced only a trace to a 
hundredth of an inch of rain upstream as precipitation falls 
into a very dry layer of air. Would expect this type of rainfall
to continue as it reaches northern New York later this 
afternoon before dwindling further as it pushes eastward. 

A break in precipitation chances will follow tonight, then 
towards midnight as the system's cold front approaches the 
International Border from the west, a vigorous piece of spin 
aloft will help increase lift and force showers to blossom. 
These showers will organize along the cold front oriented from 
southwest to northeast, and track eastward through the morning 
hours. Showers will primarily fall during the predawn hours in 
northern New York, and across northern Vermont between about 6 
and 9 AM. Following these showers, gusty west winds will mix to 
the surface with steepening near surface lapse rates. 

Widespread gusts reaching the 30 to 40 MPH range will occur 
downwind of most mountain peaks across Clinton and Essex 
counties in New York and central and eastern Vermont, with 
otherwise 25 to 30 MPH gusts common across the region with 
efficient mixing in a strong cold air advection pattern. The 
strongest gusts, especially just behind the front when the top 
of the mixed layer could tap into >40 knot winds near summit 
layer, may result in some minor impacts as leaves fall in large 
numbers. However, these winds are unlikely to produce damage or 
warrant a wind advisory given the expected magnitude of winds. 

Temperatures at 850 millibars, a proxy for our highest summit 
temperatures, will fall below freezing by tomorrow evening as 
moisture becomes very shallow. Would think some rime ice will be
possible given this set up but it cloud ice and therefore snow 
is unlikely given the expected cloud temperatures and 
saturation. Continued breezes tomorrow night should prevent 
frost conditions and limit cooling at lower elevations, but lead
to a biting cold for this time of year; wind chills will fall 
into the 20s for most locations by Tuesday morning. 

Due to a reintensification of low pressure as it wraps up into 
eastern Canada Monday night and stalls out, Tuesday will remain 
blustery with persistent westerly breezes. While winds again 
will unlikely be hazardous, there are somewhat mixed signals at 
this time range as to how strong the gust potential is. The 
consensus offers a slight weakening trend through the day and 
peak magnitude at least 5 MPH lighter than on Monday as the low 
level winds gradually weaken.

KEY MESSAGE 2: It is a tricky low temperature forecast for 
Wednesday morning as guidance has trended southward and faster 
with the progression of the next trough, which introduces return
flow earlier in the night. In general, it looks like from the 
Champlain Valley and points west, temperatures are likely to 
plummet after dark Tuesday and then stabilize or rise by 
midnight or so. Meanwhile, in much of Vermont the surface should
decouple from the milder air aloft, and this should persist 
such that low temperatures continue falling through the night 
and drop back to near or below freezing. As such, while 
widespread frost/freeze is indicated, would not expect any 
Frost/Freeze products as the growing season from our perspective
only remains in the Champlain Valley where it is looking less 
likely to see frost conditions develop. 

Breezy south winds will probably necessitate another Lake Wind 
Advisory with trends towards a deeper low passing closer to our 
region on Wednesday, not too dissimilar to today with a warm 
front pushing through our region with plentiful dry air. Only 
small chances of rain, and mainly towards the evening and 
primarily in western portions of northern New York, are being 
offered. These probabilities increase after sunset, although 
have noted the ECMWF and its ensembles have about a six hour 
earlier arrival of showers than the GEFS; timing of showers are 
fairly uncertain. Most likely high temperatures are in the upper
50s to low 60s, or roughly 10 degrees higher than the early 
week highs.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Heading into the latter half of the week, high 
pressure will shift eastward, with southerly flow allowing for 
more seasonable temperatures. Daytime high temperatures will 
climb into the upper 50s to mid 60s, with overnight lows in the 
30s to mid 40s. Throughout the week, several north stream 
systems will skirt across the region, allowing for some periods 
of light rain showers, although nothing looks significant at
